title: How do we draw the largest petals inside a square?
description: A question from the book asks how to construct four petals inside a square so that they are as big as they can be. The square is built, the midpoints of its sides are found with perpendicular bisectors, and semicircles of half the side give four petals from the centre to the corners.
teaching_notes: One idea: a semicircle on each side, with its centre at the midpoint and radius half the side, reaches both corners and the centre, and no longer radius stays inside the square. Watch for students who guess the radius by eye.

video_script.why: The child has met right angles, perpendicular bisectors and angle bisection, and has not yet put them together to draw a petal design inside a square.
video_script.substitution: The figure is built in the same way as the examples in the book: right angles for the square, perpendicular bisectors for the midpoints, and arcs drawn from a known centre.
video_script.anchor: Construct a square with four petals inside it, each petal running from the centre of the square to a corner, as large as possible.
video_script.payoff_line: The four petals are the largest possible

final_answer.value: Find the midpoints of the four sides; from each midpoint draw a semicircle of radius half the side inside the square; the four petals run from the centre to the corners and are the largest possible
final_answer.spoken: find the midpoints of the four sides, and draw a semicircle of half the side from each one; the four petals run from the centre to the corners and are the largest possible

never_show: the finished petals before step four
maths_rules: Square ABCD: right angles at A and B by equal arcs, AD = BC = AB cut with the compass, and D joined to C.
Midpoints P, Q, R, S of AB, BC, CD, DA by perpendicular bisectors; the bisectors through P and R and through Q and S cross at the centre O.
PO = half of AB, because P is the midpoint of AB and PO is perpendicular to AB with O at half the height. PA = PB = half of AB too.
A semicircle with centre P and radius PA, inside the square, passes through A, B and O. The same holds for Q, R and S.
Two neighbouring semicircles, for example from P and from Q, overlap in a petal from O to B. Four such petals run from O to A, B, C and D.
A radius longer than half the side from P would cut the sides of the square beyond the corners, so the arc leaves the square.
video_script.design: One idea: build the square, find the midpoints, draw semicircles of half the side. The picture of the book is not in the extracted text, so the petals follow the figure described by the worklist.
open_questions: The extracted book text has no readable figure for this petal question, so the petal shape follows the worklist description: a square with four petals running from the centre to the corners.
